authoredPrompt: This figure is a two-dimensional vector diagram of the allowed orientations of an orbital angular momentum vector. A vertical axis labeled z rises from an origin set at the left of the frame and is crossed there by an unlabeled horizontal axis. Seven olive-green arrows of identical length fan out from the origin into the right half of the plane, their tips landing on a dashed circular arc that makes their common magnitude explicit; the topmost arrow is labeled L with a vector arrow. A dashed horizontal line runs from each tip back to the z axis, which is ticked and labeled from top to bottom 3ħ, 2ħ, ħ, then the unlabeled origin, then -ħ, -2ħ, and -3ħ, so the arrows step in equal increments of z component rather than in equal angles. Four thin arcs of increasing radius sweep from the positive z axis to the four upper arrows and are labeled θ0 nearest the origin, then θ1, θ2, and θ3; the θ0 arc opens all the way to the horizontal arrow while the θ3 arc closes on the steepest one. Holding the arrow length fixed while stepping the projections in equal units shows that only a discrete set of polar angles is available to the vector.
authoredInteractions:
- Button / state for allowed m values: the learner steps through m = -3 to 3, one green L vector highlights at a time and its dashed projection lands on the matching hbar tick, showing that the z component is quantized while the vector length stays fixed.
- Toggle between discrete and continuous angles: the learner switches from the seven allowed vectors to a faint continuous fan, making clear that the diagram permits only selected polar angles rather than any orientation.
- Slider for quantum number l: the learner changes l, the number of allowed projection states and the common vector length update together, revealing how angular-momentum magnitude and allowed Lz values are linked.
authoredContext:
The quantization of the polar angle for the l=3 state is shown in the figure. The orbital angular momentum vector lies somewhere on the surface of a cone with an opening angle θ relative to the z-axis (unless m=0, in which case θ=90° and the vector points are perpendicular to the z-axis).

The quantization of orbital angular momentum. Each vector lies on the surface of a cone with axis along the z-axis.

Seven vector, all of the same length L, are drawn at 7 different angles to the z axis. The z components of the vectors are indicated both by horizontal lines from the tip of the vector to the z axis and by labels on the z axis. For four of the vectors, the angle between the z axis and the vector is also labeled. The z component values are 3 h bar at angle theta sub three, 2 h bar at angle theta sub two, h bar at angle theta sub one, zero at angle theta sub zero, minus h bar, minus 2 h bar, and minus 3 h bar.

A detailed study of angular momentum reveals that we cannot know all three components simultaneously. In the previous section, the z-component of orbital angular momentum has definite values that depend on the quantum number m. This implies that we cannot know both x- and y-components of angular momentum, Lx and Ly, with certainty. As a result, the precise direction of the orbital angular momentum vector is unknown.
sourceQmd: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 41: Atomic Structure

discrepancies: The selected m = 3 state is highlighted with a brighter/thicker arrow, yellow dashed guide, and green dot on the z-axis, whereas the source shows all allowed orientations uniformly without a selected-state marker.

The L vector label renders incorrectly as a boxed/garbled symbol rather than a clean vector arrow over L, and it is placed near the top vector rather than near the upper-right vector as in the source.
The generated arrows are noticeably thicker with larger cone heads than the textbook arrows, making the fan look heavier than the source.
The dashed circular locus and horizontal guides are close but slightly more compressed/right-shifted compared with the source composition.
evaluation.notes: The diagram is highly recognizable and conceptually accurate, but the selected-state embellishments and garbled L-vector label reduce fidelity to the original static figure.
action_items: Use uniform arrow color and thickness by default, or make the selected-state highlight optional/off initially to better match the source.
Replace the L-vector label with a reliably rendered label such as "\u2192L" or an HTML-styled overarrow instead of the current boxed glyph.
Slightly reduce arrow shaft/head thickness to better match the textbook figure.
Place the L label closer to the upper-right vector as in the source.
